article.title: The victory of student populism
article.author: Srđan Atanasovski
article.content: T he victory of the Student List in Serbia’s parliamentary elections on October 25, 2026 marks the end of fourteen years of domination by Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party. With approximately 53 percent of the vote and a projected absolute majority in parliament, the Student List achieved a result that until recently had seemed almost unimaginable. The nature of this victory, and Serbia’s political future, are difficult to understand through the conventional categories of government versus opposition, liberalism versus conservatism, or European integration versus national sovereignty. At the center of Serbia’s political transformation was a mass student movement, while behind it lay a conflict between two elites: the political elite built by Vučić’s regime over the previous decade and a half, and an academic elite that had remained relatively independent of his system of rule. The decisive factor was the latter’s ability to forge an alliance with the student movement, which had developed a distinctive form of participatory populism. This alliance made possible the political mobilisation that brought about the change of government. This populist movement did not emerge around demands for a radical transformation of Serbia’s economic or foreign policy. In many areas, it reproduced the existing political consensus, promising that similar policies could be pursued without corruption, organized crime, nepotism, and party based employment. The greatest challenge facing the new government will be to dismantle the previous regime’s clientelist mechanisms while demonstrating whether its relatively popular economic model can be maintained without relying on the same mechanisms of capital accumulation and political control. A one-party system within a multiparty democracy One of the most important features of Vučić’s political domination was the systematic weakening of the multiparty system, even as the formal institutions of parliamentary democracy remained in place. The Serbian Progressive Party sought to incorporate almost every political actor with significant electoral support. Political organizations and their leaders were offered positions within the governing coalition, often through guaranteed places on joint electoral lists, while those who refused to cooperate faced various forms of pressure, marginalisation, and political destruction. The result was an attempt to establish a kind of one-party system within a formally multiparty democracy. Almost every significant ideological position could be found within the governing coalition, from nationalist and conservative to liberal, pro-European, and socially oriented currents. Ideological conflicts were largely transferred from electoral competition to the internal relations of the governing bloc. Elections increasingly became referendums on the exercise of power and attitudes towards Vučić’s regime rather than contests between alternative political programs. Opposition parties that remained outside this system failed to build a sufficiently broad social base or establish a different political agenda. Vučić developed an exceptionally extensive party and electoral machine…Membership in the ruling party, or a willingness to secure votes for it, became an important prerequisite for employment, career advancement, and access to public resources. Gradually, this system extended beyond its electoral function and became a fundamental mechanism for organizing social and economic relations. At the same time, Vučić developed an exceptionally extensive party and electoral machine. Its operation depended on political loyalty, control over public-sector employment, the collection of so-called capillary votes, and various forms of pressure on voters. Membership in the ruling party, or a willingness to secure votes for it, became an important prerequisite for employment, career advancement, and access to public resources. Gradually, this system extended beyond its electoral function and became a fundamental mechanism for organizing social and economic relations. For a teacher who had spent years on temporary contracts, a healthcare worker waiting for permanent employment, or an employee of a public enterprise, party affiliation could directly determine their professional future. Similar mechanisms spread into the private sector through networks of business connections, public procurement, and privileged access to state resources. Alongside the major financial scandals reported in the media, corruption became an everyday experience for a large part of the population. Almost anyone seeking employment, career advancement, or access to a particular entitlement could encounter the consequences of party clientelism. Alongside systemic nepotism, the regime was marred by serious scandals that raised questions about links between state structures and organized crime. These included the Jovanjica case, involving the discovery of a large marijuana plantation allegedly protected by members of the security services, and a murder in a Belgrade restaurant, whose alleged cover- up implicated the then-head of the Belgrade police. The problem for Vučić was that, once established, the network of loyalty required the continuous protection of its members. Sanctioning individuals for criminal activity or corruption could threaten the stability of the entire system, which rested on the expectation that political loyalty would be rewarded and protected. The electoral machine thus gradually became a burden on the regime itself. The mechanisms that enabled it to remain in power simultaneously generated increasingly widespread social discontent. Sanctioning individuals for criminal activity or corruption could threaten the stability of the entire system…The electoral machine thus gradually became a burden on the regime itself. The academic elite Vučić failed to incorporate Unlike the political and business elites, which he successfully connected through a system of mutual interests, Vučić never managed to fully incorporate Serbia’s academic elite. By academic elite, I mean a broader stratum of highly educated professionals, professional managers, economists, lawyers, intellectuals, university professors, researchers, and people working in non-governmental organisations. Their social authority rests primarily on education, professional qualifications, and experience rather than control over the party apparatus. Throughout his rule, Vučić attempted to win over sections of this elite. Ana Brnabić’s appointment to senior government positions and the rise of Siniša Mali were important elements of this effort. Through figures such as these, individuals from business, academia, and the NGO sector were brought into the state administration and political leadership to provide the regime with professional legitimacy and an image of modernisation. This alliance remained relatively limited and unstable. Universities, led by the University of Belgrade, never became firm strongholds of the ruling party. University teachers and researchers had long expressed dissatisfaction with the regime, although this dissatisfaction was not necessarily associated with a shared opposition ideology. Shortly before the outbreak of the student protests, the conflict intensified following announcements that foreign private universities might be granted access to public funds intended for higher education. Such a model, resembling certain systems of education vouchers, raised the possibility of diverting budgetary resources from public universities to private institutions. The academic community regarded this as a threat of further subordinating education to business interests connected with political power. The conflict between universities and the regime therefore also concerned the academic community’s immediate material interests. When the canopy of the reconstructed railway station in Novi Sad collapsed in November 2024, killing sixteen people, this existing conflict acquired an entirely new dimension. The tragedy was widely perceived as emblematic of a system in which political loyalty, opaque management, and corrupt relationships displaced expertise and professional responsibility. Regardless of the specific technical causes of the collapse, the question arose of how a major infrastructure project, presented as a symbol of the country’s modernisation, could have been completed without adequate safety oversight. The student rebellion that followed received broad support from university teachers. This alliance also had a very immediate foundation: students and professors already knew one another, encountered each other daily at their faculties, and shared the same institutional space. For students, the academic elite included their own professors, with whom they could communicate and cooperate directly. Despite occasional conflicts over the blockades, universities, particularly the University of Belgrade, became crucial pillars of the movement, providing institutional, moral, and practical support. The regime responded to the rebellion by relying even more heavily on party cadres. The formation of Đuro Macut’s government, following the political crisis caused by the protests, did not bring about any meaningful reconciliation with the academic community. Figures who had failed to demonstrate sufficient party loyalty were further pushed out of government, reinforcing a system in which real political power rested within the informal party hierarchy, while ministers and other formal officeholders enjoyed limited autonomy. Student plenums and the emergence of a populist movement The student movement that emerged from the university blockades developed a distinctive organizational model based on direct democracy. Plenums were established at faculties, where students made decisions about demands, protests, and other activities. Participation in these plenums varied considerably, and informal hierarchies emerged over time. Working groups responsible for preparing proposals often acquired substantial autonomy, while plenums ratified decisions shaped by a relatively small number of active participants. As the movement continued, the number of students directly involved in everyday decision-making gradually declined. Although the organizational model of the plenums had affinities with anarchist and horizontal traditions, their political content was not revolutionary…The radicalism of the student movement lay primarily in its methods of organization and its challenge to the existing government, rather than in its ideological program. Nevertheless, the plenums retained their role as the primary source of the student movement’s legitimacy. Their importance also lay in their ability to generate broad social mobilisation. Student marches between cities, multi-day walks, cycling tours, mass demonstrations, and complex logistical operations involved large numbers of young people. Many did not necessarily participate in formulating political demands, but through organizing these activities they became active members of the movement. The student movement enabled them to become part of a broader political community through collective action, without requiring them to adopt a particular political ideology beforehand. Students carefully avoided ideological and political positions that might undermine broad social support, seeking to present themselves as a movement representing the interests of society as a whole. Although the organizational model of the plenums had affinities with anarchist and horizontal traditions, their political content was not revolutionary. Broad participation encouraged the reproduction of prevailing social attitudes, since only demands acceptable to large numbers Of participants could gain support. The radicalism of the student movement lay primarily in its methods of organization and its challenge to the existing government, rather than in its ideological program. The alliance of populism and expertise The most unusual feature of the student movement was its alliance with the academic elite. In many contemporary Western societies, populist movements develop in opposition to educated elites, experts, and professional managers. Academic institutions are often portrayed as part of an alienated establishment, removed from the everyday concerns of ordinary people. In Serbia, a mass populist movement embraced the academic elite as a natural political ally. Education, expertise, professional qualifications, and cultural capital became central elements of its political identity. This was clearly reflected in how students were presented in public. They were described as educated, decent, responsible, and capable young people: future doctors, engineers, professors, and specialists. Particular emphasis was placed on the message that they wanted to remain in Serbia and build their professional futures in their own country. This narrative corresponded directly to the experience of dissatisfaction with Vučić’s regime. In a society where employment and advancement depend on party connections, the natural alternative appears to be one in which knowledge, qualifications, and professional competence are valued. The struggle against corruption and nepotism thus became the link between the academic elite and the populist base. This alliance also involved a certain fetishisation of expertise: the expectation that people with appropriate education and professional qualifications, free from connections to the compromised political class, would be better equipped to govern the country. Such a belief overlooks the fact that expertise in a particular field does not automatically translate into political competence, and that professional elites have their own social interests, which do not always coincide with those of the majority of the population. Nevertheless, the combination of populist mobilisation and the authority of expertise enabled the student movement to move beyond the universities and become a serious political alternative. This was also reflected in the composition of the Student List. Its candidates included university professors, economists, lawyers, specialists from various fields, and a significant number of people from non-governmental organizations. Why the student movement did not develop a new ideology When the student movement decided to stop directing demands at the existing government and instead call for parliamentary elections, it took a step that might initially have appeared to abandon its original logic of direct democracy. Yet this decision was consistent with the movement’s populist character. Although based on principles of direct democracy, the student plenums reproduced another dominant social belief: that parliamentary elections are the principal mechanism of political change. At the same time, they maintained their distance from existing political parties. This was often explained by the organizational characteristics of the student movement. Since the plenums had no permanent representatives authorised to negotiate on behalf of the movement as a whole, cooperation with political parties was institutionally complicated. There was also a deeper ideological reason. The student movement could not easily negotiate a common program with parties holding clearly defined political positions. Cooperation with liberals, conservatives, nationalists, or social democrats would have required the movement to take positions on questions over which its own base was divided. Its political strength depended on its ability to avoid opening up these divisions. The Student List represented what was widely perceived in society as political normality. Its fundamental demand was for a state free from corruption, institutions that function properly, and expertise to take precedence over party affiliation. The election campaign was therefore largely free of traditional ideological conflicts. Vučić attempted to portray the Student List as a political force that would change his economic and foreign policies, jeopardise relations with Russia, or call existing social benefits into question. The Student List generally responded that such changes were not its objective and that it would implement existing policies more effectively and responsibly. There was considerably more programmatic continuity between the two largest electoral lists than the intensity of their political confrontation might suggest. The Student List represented what was widely perceived in society as political normality. Its fundamental demand was for a state free from corruption, institutions that function properly, and expertise to take precedence over party affiliation…There was considerably more programmatic continuity between the two largest electoral lists than the intensity of their political confrontation might suggest. Even when the Student List expressed opposition to the low-wage labor policy promoted by Vučić’s regime during its early years, the difference was not entirely clear. Over the preceding decade, the regime itself had attempted to move away from the image of a country attracting foreign investors exclusively through low wages, instead promoting technological development, investment in science, and more sophisticated industrial investment. There is a substantial difference between political rhetoric and actual economic outcomes, but the conflict largely concerned who was capable of realising the desired economic model. A similar logic applied to foreign policy. Vučić’s government sought to maintain relations with the European Union, Russia, and China while avoiding complete alignment with any single international bloc. This policy enjoyed relatively broad support in society, giving the Student List little reason to challenge it radically. The central electoral choice was much simpler: the continuation of a system based on party loyalty or its replacement by one promising professional governance. A referendum-like victory and the defeat of the political class The election results confirmed the strength of this political mobilisation. According to preliminary data from the Republic Electoral Commission, the Student List won 52.65 percent of the vote, while the list led by Aleksandar Vučić received 39.22 percent. Turnout was approximately 69 percent, and seat projections indicated that the Student List could form a parliamentary majority on its own. Vučić’s electoral machine managed to retain a substantial part of its voter base, but could not match the exceptionally broad mobilisation of voters seeking political change. The student movement succeeded in giving the election the character of a referendum. Voting was presented as a decision on whether the existing system of government should survive, and this atmosphere effectively eliminated the space for traditional opposition parties. Most withdrew from the electoral race, while those that remained achieved negligible results. No non-minority list other than the two dominant ones crossed the electoral threshold. The student movement thus defeated Vučić and effectively replaced the previous opposition. This may be the most important political consequence of the election. Serbia has not acquired a new governing party representing a clearly defined ideological alternative to the previous government. A movement whose legitimacy rests on the combination of mass mobilisation, rejection of corruption, and trust in expertise has secured a parliamentary majority. Real estate development: the drug fueling Vučić’s economic model Vučić’s regime survived thanks to its electoral machine and clientelist relationships, but its political stability also depended on its ability to deliver economic growth, relative stability in living standards, and increased purchasing power. The previous government’s economic policy was more complex than it is often portrayed in opposition circles. Over the preceding decade, Serbia benefited from certain advantages arising from its foreign policy position. Maintaining relations with Russia provided access to relatively affordable energy, while cooperation with China brought significant investment, particularly in industry, mining, and infrastructure. In this respect, Serbia’s economic model shared certain similarities with the policies pursued by Hungary and Slovakia. At the same time, maintaining a stable Serbian currency exchange rate against the euro was an important instrument for preserving purchasing power. For a population whose consumption depends substantially on imported goods, and for citizens with loans or other obligations denominated in euros, exchange-rate stability had immediate economic significance. The regime also sought to secure increases in pensions, public-sector wages, and various forms of social benefits. Regardless of the actual scope and distributional effects of these measures, they contributed to maintaining social support for the existing economic model. Real estate development became one of its most important pillars. Major infrastructure projects, the development of residential and commercial complexes, the Belgrade Waterfront project, preparations for EXPO, and related urban developments sustained construction activity, created jobs, and contributed to GDP growth. The problem was the economy’s excessive reliance on large, often luxury construction projects, whose contribution to economic activity largely ended when construction was completed. Moreover, a substantial share of the work was carried out by foreign companies that brought in their own workers and departed after completing the projects, leaving limited long-term benefits for the domestic economy. In Serbia, real estate development also had a distinctly political function. Major construction and infrastructure projects were among the key mechanisms linking political and business elites. Control over land, urban planning decisions, public procurement, and investment projects created opportunities for private capital accumulation. Real estate development thus became one of the mechanisms through which individuals connected to political power could themselves become capitalists. This model generated a powerful interdependence between political authority, investors, and the construction sector. Political control provided access to profitable projects, while those projects contributed to the economic growth on which the government based part of its legitimacy. Real estate development thus became one of the mechanisms through which individuals connected to political power could themselves become capitalists. This model generated a powerful interdependence between political authority, investors, and the construction sector. In this sense, real estate development became a kind of drug for Vučić’s regime. It made it possible to satisfy two important demands simultaneously: continued enrichment of the politically connected business elite and the maintenance of sufficiently high levels of economic activity for living standards to rise. Every new major project prolonged the operation of this model while increasing dependence on its continued expansion. The future of major urban development projects therefore became politically significant. The Student List’s opposition to plans for the commercial redevelopment of the General Staff complex in Belgrade, linked to the investment interests of the family of U.S. President Donald Trump, was one visible expression of the rejection of the previous approach to managing urban space and public resources. The new government will consequently face a serious problem: if it intends to dismantle the corrupt mechanisms of the previous regime, it will also have to change the way one of the economy’s important engines of growth operates. The economic constraints facing the new government The Student List presented an ambitious reform program, particularly in education, science, culture, healthcare, and social protection. This program reflects its social composition and the significant role of the academic and professional elite in shaping it. Fulfilling these promises will require substantial public resources. One assumption underlying the new government’s optimism is that combating corruption will free up sufficient resources to finance the promised reforms. More transparent public procurement, more rational investment, and reduced misuse of public funds could certainly produce substantial savings. The question remains, however, whether they will be sufficient. Even with a significant reduction in corruption, Serbia would continue to face low productivity, limited public revenues, dependence on foreign investment, and structural weaknesses in its domestic economy. The potential redirection of economic development presents a particularly complex challenge. If the new government sought to reduce dependence on real estate development and place greater emphasis on export-oriented production, it would encounter constraints arising from the existing monetary and economic model. Strengthening the competitiveness of domestic agriculture and certain industrial sectors, for example, could raise questions about the real value of the dinar. Depreciation of the domestic currency might improve the price competitiveness of exports, but it would also make imported goods more expensive and undermine purchasing power. Such a move would not automatically solve problems in production and could have serious social consequences. Preserving purchasing power was one of the Student List’s important promises. Its populist base does not expect an economic policy that asks citizens to accept declining living standards in the name of long-term development goals. Similar constraints apply to the emigration of young and educated people. Over the previous two years, the student movement strongly emphasised that young people wanted to remain in Serbia and build their futures there. Yet the emigration of educated workers is not exclusively a consequence of corruption or authoritarian government. Croatia’s experience demonstrates that even EU member states can face large-scale labor emigration, while freedom of movement within the European labor market can make migration to wealthier countries easier. The new government will therefore face a range of problems for which there are no simple technical solutions. Its response to the question of future economic development centers primarily on increasing productivity, one of the most difficult tasks of economic policy, requiring long-term structural change rather than merely replacing political personnel. Will the populist base control the new elite? The most important question following the electoral victory concerns the relationship the new government will establish with the movement that brought it to power. Over the previous two years, student plenums had been the primary source of the movement’s legitimacy. They decided on political demands, forms of mobilisation, and ultimately the move into parliamentary politics. The process of compiling the Student List further demonstrated the movement’s insistence on controlling its representatives. Candidates underwent lengthy procedures to scrutinise their biographies and professional integrity, with the aim of preventing the nomination of individuals whose past could compromise the entire movement. This approach reflected the fundamental political message that power should be entrusted to competent and uncompromised individuals. The entry of approximately 140 Student List representatives into parliament creates an entirely new situation. MPs will now possess formal political legitimacy, access to state institutions, and the ability to participate directly in decision-making. They will no longer be merely delegates of a protest movement, but holders of parliamentary mandates. The question is whether the new government will continue to recognise the authority of student plenums and other participatory forms of organization. The plenums themselves have already weakened considerably: their activity is declining, and fewer students are participating. If they manage to preserve their organizational structures and connections with elected representatives, they could function as a mechanism of social control over the new government, limiting the autonomy of professional administrators and their ability to pursue policies contrary to the expectations of the movement’s electoral base. There is also the possibility that the connection with the student movement will gradually be severed. In that case, the academic elite, which already occupies a prominent position within the Student List, could become the dominant political force in the new government. Its representatives might begin to behave like professional political and managerial elites in Western societies, justifying unpopular measures through appeals to economic necessity, fiscal responsibility, or market demands. The Student List’s MPs hold a range of political convictions. Some are closer to liberal and pro- European positions, others to conservative or nationalist ones, while some candidates are associated with socially oriented policies. As long as the main objective was to remove Vučić’s regime, these differences did not have to become politically decisive. Once the new government faces concrete questions of taxation, privatisation, public spending, labor legislation, and international relations, ideological conflicts may become unavoidable. It is easy to imagine liberal, conservative, nationalist, or left-wing groupings gradually emerging within the parliamentary majority. Such a development would mark the end of the distinctive populist unity that made electoral victory possible and could open the way to neoliberal reforms, austerity policies, or other measures that directly threaten the living standards of sections of the population. Between political normalisation and a new democracy The Student List’s victory demonstrated that even an exceptionally sophisticated party machine can be defeated through broad social mobilisation. The student movement united a large part of the population around demands to end corruption, nepotism, and party control over institutions. Its fundamental promise was one of political normalisation. The immediate consequences of this victory are already visible. From the perspective of Radnički glas (Workers’ Voice), an organization of which I am a member and which works with trade unions in education, research, culture, and other sectors, the change in political relations was felt practically overnight. Just one day after the election, we are already observing changes in the behavior of certain directors and managers, while questions are emerging about the future of numerous proceedings initiated against employees who opposed the government. A military trade union that announced several months ago that it was ceasing its activities because of political pressure has now issued a new statement, suggesting that it may resume its work. Party nepotism was an everyday experience for large numbers of employees. For many people, the Student List’s victory therefore brings a sense of liberation from immediate pressure. The possibility of speaking more freely at work, refusing a political instruction, or planning a professional future without dependence on party loyalty represents a tangible change. This helps explain the mass celebrations following the election. The victory has also opened up the possibility of transforming political representation itself. Here we encounter perhaps the most interesting, and seemingly paradoxical, similarity between the Student List and Vučić’s regime. Both, in different ways, displaced the traditional multiparty system based on competition between ideologically defined parties. Vučić incorporated different political options into his governing coalition, subordinating them to the party apparatus and its hierarchy. The Student List brought together ideologically diverse representatives around a common political objective, but built their legitimacy through mass participation rather than a traditional party organization. The absence of clearly defined party programs need not be a weakness of the new political order. Competition between political parties, in which citizens periodically choose between pre- formulated programs, is not the only possible form of democratic representation. The student movement demonstrated that enormous numbers of people who had never belonged to political parties or previously engaged in political activism could be mobilised. Their participation extended beyond protests to organizing the election campaign, protecting polling stations, and directly monitoring the electoral process. People who had previously been merely voters became active participants in political life. The question is whether this form of participation can be sustained after the electoral victory. Student plenums have already weakened, but the social energy released by the movement need not remain tied exclusively to them. It is particularly significant that many Student List candidates are professionally established individuals with no previous political ambitions. Their willingness to accept parliamentary mandates does not necessarily imply a desire to become professional politicians. Understanding political office as a temporary social responsibility could help establish a different relationship between representatives and those they represent. Trade unions could play an important role in this process. Unlike student plenums, whose activity is linked to the changing composition of the student population, trade unions have more durable organizational structures, direct connections with employees, and concrete demands arising from everyday employment relations. In the political space opening up after the fall of the previous regime, they could establish themselves as one of the organized voices from below. This would also entail a different relationship with parliamentary power. Trade unions would not have to confine themselves to traditional social dialogue, appeals to ministries, and occasional negotiations with government officials. They could establish lasting connections with Student List MPs, following the example of the cooperation they developed with student plenums during the protests, and use these relationships to articulate workers’ demands and exert pressure on the government. Implementing the promises made in the student program, including the expansion of labor rights, could provide a common framework for such action, while unions preserve their independence and their role as the organized voice of workers. Such a relationship could offer a way beyond the limitations of representative parliamentary democracy. Organized social groups could participate directly in shaping political decisions and overseeing their implementation. Parliament could then become a place where the demands of the social base are articulated, rather than an institution in which professional politicians make decisions independently between electoral cycles. The most important possibility opened up by the Student List’s victory lies in the opportunity to free political representation from its exclusive dependence on party competition and to build a more lasting connection between elected representatives and an active, organized society. The student movement has already demonstrated that mass political participation can exist outside traditional political parties. Its next challenge will be to show whether that participation can endure when representatives of the movement constitute the governing parliamentary majority.
